title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 128
paragraphs: When Astyages had been made prisoner, Harpagos came and stood near him and exulted over him and mocked him. Among other things he said to grieve him, he asked in particular how it pleased him to be a slave instead of a king, making reference to that dinner at which Astyages had feasted him on the flesh of his own son. Astyages, looking at him, asked in return whether he claimed the work of Cyrus as his own deed. Harpagos said that since he had written the letter, the deed was justly his. Then Astyages declared him to be at the same time the most unskillful and the most unjust of men: the most unskillful because, when it was in his power to become king himself (as it was, if the thing now done had really been brought about by him), he had conferred the chief power on another; and the most unjust, because on account of that dinner he had reduced the Medes to slavery. For if he had to confer the kingdom on some other and not keep it himself, it was more just to give this good thing to one of the Medes rather than to one of the Persians. But as things stood, the Medes, who were guiltless in this matter, had become slaves instead of masters, and the Persians, who formerly were slaves of the Medes, had now become their masters.
